name: Idempotency
intent: Make an operation safe to repeat, so that doing it twice (because of a retry, a double click or a redelivered message) has the same effect as doing it once.
scenario: A customer taps 'Pay $50'. The charge succeeds, but the response is lost on a bad mobile connection. The app times out and retries. Without protection, the customer is charged $100.
problem: Networks cannot tell you whether a request that timed out was processed or not. To be reliable, clients must retry, and message brokers redeliver. So the same request will sometimes arrive more than once, and operations like 'charge', 'send email' or 'create order' must not repeat their side effects.

howItWorks.title: Some operations are naturally idempotent
howItWorks.text: 'Set the status to shipped' or 'delete order 42' give the same result however many times you run them. 'Add $50 to the balance' or 'append a row' do not. Prefer the first kind when you can.

howItWorks.title: The client sends an idempotency key
howItWorks.text: For operations that are not naturally safe, the client generates a unique key (for example a UUID) when the user takes the action and sends it with the request, often in an Idempotency-Key header. Every retry of that action reuses the same key.

howItWorks.title: The server records the result under the key
howItWorks.text: On the first request the server does the work and stores the key together with the response. The check and the work must be atomic, for example in one database transaction or with a unique constraint, so two simultaneous requests cannot both pass.

howItWorks.title: Repeats get the stored answer
howItWorks.text: If a request arrives with a key the server has seen, it skips the work and returns the saved response. The client cannot tell the difference, which is the point.

howItWorks.title: Expire keys and reject mismatches
howItWorks.text: Keys are kept for a window (often 24 hours) and then removed. If the same key arrives with a different body, that is a client bug, and the server should return an error rather than guess.

pros: Makes retries, redelivery and double clicks safe
Lets clients retry aggressively without fear of duplicate effects
Turns at-least-once delivery into effectively-once processing
Simple concept that works across HTTP, queues and jobs
cons: Needs storage for keys and results, and a cleanup policy
The check-and-process step must be atomic, which is easy to get wrong
Clients must generate and persist keys correctly
Side effects outside your database (an email, a call to a third party) need the same care
whenToUse: Payments, orders and anything that moves money or stock
Message handlers fed by an at-least-once queue
Any API where clients will retry on timeout
Webhooks, which providers often deliver more than once
whenNotToUse: Reads and operations that are already naturally idempotent
Cases where each repeat should count (a counter of page views)
pitfalls: Generating a new key on every retry, which defeats the whole mechanism
Checking for the key and then processing in separate steps, so concurrent duplicates both pass
Storing the key only after the side effect, so a crash in between creates a duplicate
Using a key that is not unique per action, for example the user id alone

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Sends the request with an idempotency key and may retry.

roles.label: Server
roles.description: Checks the key, does the work once and replays the result.

roles.label: Key store
roles.description: Remembers each key with its response.

quiz.question: A mobile app sends POST /payments with an Idempotency-Key header. The request times out, so the app retries. Which key should the retry carry?
options: A new random UUID, so the server treats the retry as a fresh, independent request
The same key as the first attempt, since both are one user action
The user id, since the same user is paying and the server can recognise them
The retry timestamp, so the server can tell which attempt arrived last
quiz.explanation: The key identifies the action, so every retry of it must reuse the key. A new key per attempt defeats the protection, and the user id would block that user's next, different payment.

quiz.question: A payments endpoint first runs SELECT to see if the idempotency key exists. If not, it charges the card and then inserts the key. A double tap sends two identical requests within 5 ms to different servers, and the customer is charged twice. What is the best fix?
options: Cache the keys in each server's memory so that the check is faster than the charge
Run the key check twice, 10 ms apart, and only charge if both checks find nothing
Add a 1 second delay after the first request so the key is stored before the second arrives
Insert the key under a unique constraint first, in the same transaction as the work, so one request wins
quiz.explanation: The check and the write must be atomic. A unique constraint lets the database decide which request wins. Per-server memory cannot see the other server, and delays or double checks only narrow the race.

quiz.question: A server charges a card through a payment provider, then saves the idempotency key and result. It crashes after the charge but before saving. The client retries with the same key. The provider supports idempotency keys. What is the best design?
options: Save the key as in progress first, then pass it to the provider to dedupe a retry
Wrap the charge and the key save in one database transaction, so a crash rolls the charge back and the retry starts clean
Keep the key for 30 days instead of 24 hours, so the retry always finds it
Ask the client to wait 5 minutes before retrying so the server has time to recover
quiz.explanation: The charge happens at an outside system, so a local transaction cannot undo it. Writing the key first and passing it on lets the provider dedupe the retry. A longer retention window does nothing for a key that was never saved.
